claims.claim: For the reflection functor F⁺ᵢ, the linear maps in Q̄ᵢ out of vertex i (i.e., reversed arrows from i to j ≠ i) are given by the composition: ker(φ) ↪ ⊕_{j→i} V_j → V_j (inclusion of kernel then projection onto the j-component).

The declaration is non-sorry and non-vacuous.

claims.claim: For a Dynkin quiver, there are only finitely many indecomposable representations (up to isomorphism).
claims.reason: Theorem_6_5_2a_finiteness (Theorem6_5_2.lean, line 159) proves Set.Finite {d | IsPositiveRoot n adj d}. Combined with Theorem_6_5_2c_bijection (line 215), which gives a bijection between positive roots and isomorphism classes of indecomposables for any Dynkin orientation, the finiteness of indecomposable isomorphism classes follows. The Problem6_1_5_theorem.lean (Etingof.Theorem_6_1_5) assembles this into IsFiniteTypeQuiver for the Dynkin direction. All non-sorry.

claims.claim: The dimension vector of every indecomposable representation of a Dynkin quiver is a positive root (i.e., B(d,d)=2, d≥0, d≠0).
claims.reason: Etingof.Corollary6_8_2 in Corollary6_8_2.lean proves exactly this: given that d is the dimension vector of an indecomposable representation of a Dynkin quiver (encoded via hreflect), IsPositiveRoot n adj d holds. Non-sorry.

claims.source_span: It appears as if the number of indecomposable representations does not depend on the orientation of the edges — and indeed Gabriel's theorem will generalize this observation.
claims.claim: For a fixed Dynkin graph, different orientations have the same number of indecomposable representations (up to isomorphism).
claims.reason: This is an informal observation and forward-pointer to Gabriel's theorem. The underlying formal content is covered by Theorem_6_5_2c_bijection: for any orientation Q of the Dynkin graph adj, the set of indecomposable isomorphism classes bijects with {positive roots of adj}. Since the positive roots are independent of the orientation Q (they depend only on adj), any two orientations have the same count. The orientation-independence itself is not stated as a standalone theorem, but it is an immediate consequence of Theorem_6_5_2c_bijection and the orientation-independence of IsPositiveRoot. The blob text is explicitly informal ('it appears as if') and framed as motivation. Verdict: covered rather than genuine_gap.

claims.source_span: This sequence is well defined because of the selected labeling: $n$ has to be a sink of $Q$, $n-1$ has to be a sink of $\overline{Q}_n$ (where $\overline{Q}_r$ is obtained from $Q$ by reversing all the arrows at the vertex $r$) and so on.
claims.claim: Every Dynkin quiver orientation admits an admissible ordering (labeling) such that each vertex is a sink of the quiver obtained after reversing all previous vertices in the ordering.
claims.reason: Etingof.admissibleOrdering_exists in CoxeterInfrastructure.lean (line 636) proves exactly this: ∃ ordering, IsAdmissibleOrdering Q ordering, where IsAdmissibleOrdering requires each vertex ordering[k] to be a sink of iteratedReversedAtVertices Q (ordering.take k). Non-sorry.

claims.source_span: Furthermore, we note that $V^{(n)}$ is a representation of $Q$ again, since every arrow has been reversed twice (since we applied a reflection functor to every vertex).
claims.claim: Reversing all arrows at all n vertices of a quiver (one for each vertex) returns the quiver to its original state.
claims.reason: Theorem iteratedReversedAtVertices_perm_eq in CoxeterInfrastructure.lean (line 525) proves: for any permutation σ of all vertices, iteratedReversedAtVertices Q σ = Q. The proof notes each edge gets reversed twice (once for each endpoint). Non-sorry.
